title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
statement: Given the daily prices of one share, you may buy and sell as many times as you like, but you may hold at most one share at a time and you may not buy on the day immediately after a sale — selling forces a one-day cooldown. Return the maximum profit obtainable.
realWorld: Any policy over time with a lockout after an action: a trading strategy with a settlement period, a rate limiter that forces a quiet window after a burst, an autoscaler that must wait a cycle after scaling down, or a machine that needs a cleaning pass between jobs. The cooldown is what turns a simple scan into a state machine.

examples.explanation: Buy at 1, sell at 2 (+1), cooldown on day 2, buy at 0, sell at 2 (+2). Total 3. Without the cooldown the answer would be 4, so the constraint really bites.
Buy at 1 and hold all the way to 7 for +6. Trading twice — 1 to 3 and 2 to 4 or 7 — loses a day to the cooldown and nets less, so the greedy 'take every rise' rule fails here.
Nothing can be completed, so the best profit is zero — never a negative number, since doing nothing is always allowed.

constraints: At most one share may be held at a time
After any sale, the next day cannot be a buying day

bruteForce.idea: Recurse over the days. On each day, do nothing, or take the one action the current situation allows: buy if you are free to buy, sell if you are holding. After a sale, skip a day before the search may buy again.
code: private static int best(int[] prices, int day, boolean holding) {
int sellToday = prices[day] + best(prices, day + 2, false);   // +2 is the cooldown
bruteForce.whySlow: Two choices a day gives about 2^n paths — 10^9 by day 30, against 5000 days in the constraints. Yet the situation the recursion is actually in is fully described by two things: which day it is, and whether a share is held. That is 2n distinct situations in the whole problem. 'Best profit from day 12 onwards, holding nothing' is recomputed once for every one of the thousands of trading histories that arrive at day 12 empty-handed, and it returns the same number every single time.

patternIdentification: When the constraint is about what you are ALLOWED TO DO NEXT rather than about a quantity, the state is not an index — it is (index, mode). Enumerate the modes the process can be in at the end of a day, draw the legal arrows between consecutive days, and every arrow becomes one term of one recurrence. Here there are three modes: HELD (owning a share), SOLD (sold today, so tomorrow is a cooldown) and REST (owning nothing and free to buy). The arrows are: HELD comes from HELD (keep holding) or from REST minus today's price (buy) — and never from SOLD, which is exactly where the cooldown lives; SOLD comes only from HELD plus today's price, because selling is the only way to be in it; REST comes from REST (stay idle) or from SOLD (yesterday's cooldown has expired). Base cases are day 0: held = -prices[0], sold = 0, rest = 0. The answer is max(sold, rest) on the last day — never held, since an unsold share is money spent for nothing. This shape generalises far beyond stocks: as soon as a problem has a lockout, a limited number of transactions, or an on/off mode, stop trying to bend a single dp array around it and model the modes explicitly.

optimized.idea: Carry one number per mode and step them forward day by day. Each new value is computed from yesterday's three values, so snapshot them before the updates. The whole table is three ints wide regardless of how many days there are.
code: int held = -prices[0];   // holding a share, having paid for it
int sold = 0;            // sold today, so tomorrow is a cooldown
int rest = 0;            // holding nothing and free to buy
int prevHeld = held, prevSold = sold, prevRest = rest;
held = Math.max(prevHeld, prevRest - prices[i]);   // buying is legal only from rest
return Math.max(sold, rest);   // never held: an unsold share is not profit

commonMistakes: Letting a buy happen straight out of the sold state — held = max(prevHeld, max(prevRest, prevSold) - price). The cooldown vanishes and the code silently solves the unrestricted version: [1,2,3,0,2] returns 4 instead of 3, which is exactly the answer to the wrong problem.

Updating held, sold and rest in place instead of from a snapshot of yesterday's values. sold then reads the held that was already advanced this iteration, so one day's transition is applied twice and [1,2,3,0,2] also returns 4 — the same wrong number as the missing-cooldown bug, which makes it easy to misdiagnose as a cooldown problem when it is really an aliasing problem.

Initialising held = 0 rather than -prices[0]. The first purchase becomes free and every answer is inflated by exactly prices[0] whenever day 0 is the first buy: [1,2,3,0,2] returns 4 instead of 3, and the error scales with how expensive the first day happened to be.
